entries.title: Cherokee at a glance
body: Cherokee (ᏣᎳᎩ, Tsalagi) is an Iroquoian language of the Cherokee people, spoken today mainly in Oklahoma and in the Qualla Boundary in North Carolina. It has about 2,000 first-language speakers, most of them elders, and the Cherokee Nation, the Eastern Band and the United Keetoowah Band all run immersion schools and language programmes.

Cherokee builds long words from a verb root with many prefixes and suffixes. A single verb can say who does what to whom, when, and how the speaker knows it, so a whole English sentence is often one Cherokee word.

entries.title: Sequoyah's syllabary
body: Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith who did not read any other language, created the syllabary in the 1810s and it was adopted by the Cherokee Nation in 1825. Within a few years a large share of Cherokee people could read and write it, and the newspaper Cherokee Phoenix was printed in it from 1828.

Each of its 85 characters (86 in the original) stands for a syllable: a consonant plus a vowel, or a vowel alone. The six vowels are a, e, i, o, u and v, a nasal “uh” sound. Some letters look like Latin letters but have unrelated sounds: Ꭰ is a, Ꭱ is e, and Ꮃ is la.

entries.title: The seven clans
body: Traditional Cherokee society has seven clans, passed down through the mother: Wolf (ᎠᏂᏩᏯ, Aniwaya), Deer (Anikawi), Bird (Anitsiskwa), Paint (Aniwodi), Long Hair (Anigilohi), Blue (Anisahoni) and Wild Potato (Anigatogewi).
Seven is an important number in Cherokee tradition, and the seven-pointed star appears on the seal of the Cherokee Nation.

entries.title: Set A prefixes on “is speaking”
entries.body: Most Cherokee verbs need a bound pronoun on the front. Set A prefixes mark who is doing the action on verbs like ᎦᏬᏂᎭ (gawoniha) “is speaking”. The independent pronouns ᎠᏴ (ayv) “I” and ᏂᎯ (nihi) “you” are only added for emphasis.

entries.title: Set B “want”, and “go”
entries.body: Some verbs take Set B prefixes instead. “Want” is one of them: ᎠᏆᏚᎵᎭ (agwaduliha) “I want it”, ᏣᏚᎵᎭ (tsaduliha) “you want it”, ᎤᏚᎵᎭ (uduliha) “he / she wants it”. “Go” is a short stem: ᎨᎦ (gega) “I am going”, ᎮᎦ (hega) “you are going”.

entries.title: Questions: ‑Ꮝ and question words
entries.body: A yes/no question often adds ‑Ꮝ (-s) or ‑Ꮷ (-tsu) to the first word. Content questions start with a question word: ᎦᏙ (gado) “what”, ᎦᎪ (gago) “who”, ᎭᏢ (hadlv) “where”.

entries.title: Negation with Ꮭ
entries.body: Western Cherokee puts Ꮭ (tla) “not” before the verb and adds a negation prefix on the verb: yi- before a consonant, y- before a vowel. Eastern materials often write ᎨᏍᏗ (gesdi) for the same “not”.

entries.title: Cherokee Phoenix
body: The Cherokee Phoenix (ᏣᎳᎩ ᏧᎴᎯᏌᏅᎯ, Tsalagi Tsulehisanvhi) began printing in New Echota in 1828, in Sequoyah’s syllabary and in English. It was the first newspaper published by a Native American nation.
The press helped spread literacy in the syllabary across the Cherokee Nation before Removal. A modern Cherokee Phoenix still publishes from Tahlequah, Oklahoma.
